name: Cybersecurity for AI Devices
blurb: The FDA's premarket cybersecurity expectations as they apply to AI.
title: Cybersecurity for AI Devices
answer: Connected and AI enabled devices must show cybersecurity risk management in their premarket submissions, including a software bill of materials and plans for patching. AI adds its own attack surface, from poisoned training data to manipulated inputs, which should be part of the same threat model.

reading.body:
The FDA treats cybersecurity as premarket content for connected and AI enabled devices, not a post-market afterthought.

The expectation is concrete: cybersecurity risk management in the submission, a software bill of materials, and a plan for patching. Those are documentation and process requirements, and they apply before a device reaches a patient rather than after a vulnerability is found.

AI changes the threat model that documentation has to cover. Poisoned training data, manipulated inputs and model theft sit alongside the conventional device attack surface, and the data's guidance is to add them from the start rather than bolt them on. For a medtech team this is a scoping decision made early, when the threat model is written, because a submission built around network security alone will not describe the model specific risks.

What this does not cover is the substance of the guidance itself. There is one dated development, the 2023 FDA cybersecurity guidance, and no detail on submission formats, review timelines, or how any of it has been enforced. It also says nothing about compute, buildings or power, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

sections.body: Add model specific threats, data poisoning, adversarial inputs and model theft, to the device threat model from the start.
